questions.q: The parts of the stomach are:
opts: Cardia, fundus, body, antrum and pylorus
questions.exp: Parts of stomach: cardia, fundus, body, antrum, pylorus. (Book p150)

questions.q: The left gastric artery is a branch of the:
questions.exp: Left gastric artery: branch of the coeliac axis. (Book p150)

questions.q: The dominant artery of the stomach is the:
questions.exp: Left gastric artery: dominant artery of the stomach. (Book p150)

questions.q: The artery involved in a type IV gastric ulcer and in a Mallory Weiss tear is the:
questions.exp: Left gastric artery: involved in type IV gastric ulcer and Mallory Weiss tear. (Book p150)

questions.q: The right gastric artery is a branch of the:
questions.exp: Right gastric artery: branch of the common hepatic artery. (Book p150)

questions.q: The right gastroepiploic artery is a branch of the:
questions.exp: Right gastroepiploic artery: branch of the gastroduodenal artery. (Book p150)

questions.q: The short gastric arteries are branches of the:
questions.exp: Short gastric arteries: branches of the splenic artery. (Book p150)

questions.q: The stomach tolerates ligation of several of its arteries because of:
opts: Extensive submucosal anastomoses between the vessels
Collaterals from the superior mesenteric artery
questions.exp: Extensive submucosal anastomosis between the vessels - the stomach does not necrose even if vessels are ligated. (Book p150)

questions.q: The veins of the stomach:
opts: Drain entirely into the inferior vena cava
questions.exp: Venous supply: veins corresponding to the arteries. (Book p151)

questions.q: The vein responsible for metastases into the liver from the stomach is the:
questions.exp: Left gastric vein / coronary vein: responsible for metastases into the liver. (Book p151)

questions.q: Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is also known as:
questions.exp: CHPS: AKA idiopathic hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. (Book p151)

questions.q: The pathophysiology of CHPS is thickened pyloric muscle leading to:
questions.exp: Thickened pyloric muscle → gastric outlet obstruction → vomiting. (Book p151)

questions.q: CHPS m/c affects:
questions.exp: Features: m/c affects the first born male child. (Book p151)

questions.q: CHPS is associated with all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Associations: Apert syndrome, Cornelia de Lange syndrome, decreased nitric oxide synthase levels, erythromycin intake early in life. (Book p151)

questions.q: Nitric oxide synthase levels in CHPS are:
questions.exp: Association: decreased nitric oxide synthase levels. (Book p151)

questions.q: Infants with CHPS are typically asymptomatic for the:
questions.exp: Presentation: asymptomatic during the first 2-3 weeks, followed by projectile non-bilious vomiting. (Book p151)

questions.q: The characteristic vomiting of CHPS is:
questions.exp: Projectile, non-bilious vomiting is the hallmark of CHPS. (Book p151)

questions.q: The abdominal examination in CHPS is best performed:
questions.exp: Examination: best done during feeding; palpate an olive shaped swelling. (Book p151)

questions.q: The palpable mass in CHPS is described as:
questions.exp: Olive shaped swelling is palpated in CHPS. (Book p151)

questions.q: Visible peristalsis in CHPS moves:
questions.exp: Peristalsis: visible, left to right. (Book p151)

questions.q: Unlike CHPS, duodenal atresia presents with:
opts: Non bilious projectile vomiting after a few weeks
questions.exp: Duodenal atresia: bilious vomiting since birth; CHPS: non-bilious projectile vomiting after a few weeks. (Book p152)

questions.q: The X-ray sign of duodenal atresia is:
questions.exp: Duodenal atresia: X-ray shows the double bubble sign. (Book p152)

questions.q: The investigation of choice for CHPS is:
questions.exp: Evaluation: IOC is USG. (Book p152)

questions.q: The ultrasound criterion for pyloric muscle thickness in CHPS is:
questions.exp: USG: thickness >= 4 mm and increased pyloric channel length. (Book p152)

questions.q: The contrast study findings in CHPS include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Contrast study: string sign, mushroom sign, double tract sign. (Book p152)

questions.q: The plain X-ray finding in CHPS is:
questions.exp: X-ray: single bubble sign. (Book p152)

questions.q: The metabolic abnormality in CHPS results from loss of:
questions.exp: CHPS: loss of HCl due to vomiting (loss of H+ and Cl-). (Book p152)

questions.q: The acid base disturbance in CHPS is:
questions.exp: Loss of H+ and Cl- produces a metabolic alkalosis. (Book p152)

questions.q: Initially, the kidney compensates for the metabolic alkalosis of CHPS by:
opts: Increased elimination of NaHCO3 in the urine
questions.exp: Compensatory increase in elimination of NaHCO3 in the urine. (Book p152)

questions.q: Aldosterone release in CHPS occurs through activation of:
questions.exp: Activation of RAS (renin angiotensin system) causes aldosterone release. (Book p152)

questions.q: Paradoxical aciduria in CHPS means:
opts: Acidic urine despite systemic metabolic alkalosis
questions.exp: H+ ions are eliminated in the urine initially with secretion of K+ into urine: paradoxical aciduria. (Book p152)

questions.q: The electrolyte and acid base picture in CHPS is:
opts: Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypochloremia, metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria
Hyperkalemia, hypernatremia, hyperchloremia and metabolic acidosis
questions.exp: Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypochloremia, metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. (Book p152)

questions.q: The intravenous fluid used for resuscitation in CHPS is:
questions.exp: Management: Ringer lactate. (Book p153)

questions.q: After an uneventful Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy, feeding is started at:
questions.exp: Uneventful surgery: feeding started in 4-6 hrs. (Book p153)

questions.q: If the mucosa is injured during pyloromyotomy, feeding is started at:
questions.exp: Mucosal injury: feeding started in 24-48 hrs. (Book p153)

questions.q: The operation performed for CHPS is:
questions.exp: Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy: muscle is split and the mucosa bulges out. (Book p153)

questions.q: The m/c peptic ulcer is:
questions.exp: Peptic ulcers: duodenal ulcer is the m/c type. (Book p153)

questions.q: The proportion of duodenal ulcers attributable to H. pylori is:
questions.exp: Duodenal ulcer: 90-95% due to H. pylori. (Book p153)

questions.q: The proportion of gastric ulcers attributable to H. pylori is:
questions.exp: Gastric ulcer: 60-65% due to H. pylori. (Book p153)

questions.q: Duodenal ulcers are characterised by:
questions.exp: Duodenal ulcer: acid hypersecretion. (Book p153)

questions.q: Type I and type II gastric ulcers are associated with:
questions.exp: Gastric ulcer type I and II: normal acid production. (Book p153)

questions.q: The m/c site of a duodenal ulcer is:
questions.exp: Duodenal ulcers: m/c site is D1, the first part of the duodenum. (Book p153)

questions.q: Pain of a duodenal ulcer is classically:
questions.exp: Duodenal ulcer: upper abdominal pain relieved with food. (Book p153)

questions.q: The m/c complication of a peptic ulcer is:
questions.exp: Complications: bleeding is the m/c. (Book p154)

questions.q: Bleeding from a duodenal ulcer commonly arises from a:
questions.exp: Bleeding: posterior ulcers are commonly involved. (Book p154)

questions.q: The vessel implicated in bleeding from a duodenal ulcer is the:
questions.exp: Implicated vessel: gastroduodenal artery. (Book p154)

questions.q: Peptic ulcer disease is the m/c cause of:
questions.exp: Bleeding peptic ulcer: m/c cause of upper GI hemorrhage. (Book p154)

questions.q: First line management of a bleeding peptic ulcer is:
opts: Endoscopic management with adrenaline and coagulation
questions.exp: Management: endoscopic management - adrenaline, coagulation. (Book p154)

questions.q: After a re-bleed from a peptic ulcer, the next step is:
questions.exp: Re-bleeds: second trial of endoscopy. (Book p154)

questions.q: If endoscopic management of a bleeding peptic ulcer fails, the treatment is:
opts: Surgery with under-running (ligation) of the vessel
questions.exp: If endoscopy fails: surgery and under-run the vessel (ligate). (Book p154)

questions.q: After a bleeding peptic ulcer is controlled, the additional step advised is:
questions.exp: Once bleeding stops: H. pylori eradication. (Book p154)

questions.q: Perforation of a duodenal ulcer is m/c seen with:
questions.exp: Perforation: anterior ulcers (m/c). (Book p154)

questions.q: Perforation of an anterior duodenal ulcer presents with:
opts: Peritonitis with guarding, rigidity and rebound tenderness
questions.exp: Anterior ulcer perforation: peritonitis - rebound tenderness, guarding, rigidity. (Book p154)

questions.q: The X-ray finding in a perforated peptic ulcer is:
questions.exp: X-ray: gas under the diaphragm (hollow viscus perforation). (Book p154)

questions.q: The initial management of perforation peritonitis includes all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: IV antibiotics with aerobic and anaerobic cover
questions.exp: Management of perforation peritonitis: IV fluids, preparation for emergency laparotomy, IV antibiotics (aerobic + anaerobic cover), analgesics. (Book p154)

questions.q: The definitive surgery for a perforated duodenal ulcer is:
questions.exp: Definitive management: omental patch repair / Graham's patch repair. (Book p154)

questions.q: A posterior duodenal ulcer that perforates does so into the:
questions.exp: Posterior ulcer (rare): perforates into the retroperitoneum. (Book p154)

questions.q: Valentino syndrome, seen with a leaking posterior duodenal ulcer, mimics:
questions.exp: Valentino syndrome: mimics acute appendicitis. (Book p154)

questions.q: Kocherisation is done in posterior duodenal ulcer surgery to:
opts: Mobilise the duodenum to visualise the posterior ulcer
questions.exp: Kocherisation: mobilisation of the duodenum to view the posterior ulcer. (Book p154)

questions.q: Johnson's type I gastric ulcer is located:
opts: Along the lesser curvature close to the incisura
High in the body of the stomach
questions.exp: Type I: m/c type, along the lesser curvature (close to the incisura). (Book p155)

questions.q: The m/c type of gastric ulcer in Johnson's classification is:
questions.exp: Type I is the m/c type of gastric ulcer. (Book p155)

questions.q: Johnson's type II gastric ulcer is:
opts: A prepyloric ulcer associated with a duodenal ulcer
An ulcer high in the body
questions.exp: Type II: prepyloric ulcer plus duodenal ulcer. (Book p155)

questions.q: Johnson's type III gastric ulcer is located:
questions.exp: Type III: prepyloric ulcer. (Book p155)

questions.q: Johnson's type IV gastric ulcer is located:
opts: High up in the body of the stomach
questions.exp: Type IV: high up in the body; the left gastric artery is the implicated vessel. (Book p155)

questions.q: Type IV gastric ulcers characteristically bleed from the:
questions.exp: Type IV: vessel is the left gastric artery; bleeds. (Book p155)

questions.q: Johnson's type V gastric ulcer is caused by:
questions.exp: Type V: NSAID induced ulcer, diffuse. (Book p155)

questions.q: Bleeding is a feature mainly of Johnson's type:
questions.exp: Type IV and V: bleeding +/-. (Book p155)

questions.q: Pain in a gastric ulcer classically:
questions.exp: Clinical features: pain worsens with food. (Book p155)

questions.q: The m/c complication of a gastric ulcer is:
questions.exp: Gastric ulcer: m/c complication is perforation. (Book p155)

questions.q: The investigation used to diagnose a gastric ulcer is:
questions.exp: Diagnosis: upper GI endoscopy. (Book p155)

questions.q: The U or J manoeuvre during endoscopy is done to visualise:
questions.exp: U or J manoeuvre: to visualise a fundal ulcer. (Book p155)

questions.q: All gastric ulcers should be biopsied because:
opts: Of the risk of an underlying cancer
H. pylori can only be seen on biopsy
It is the only way to stop bleeding
questions.exp: All gastric ulcers should be biopsied (risk of cancer). (Book p155)

questions.q: The vessel most often implicated in bleeding from a gastric ulcer is the:
questions.exp: Gastric ulcer bleeding: left gastric artery; peptic (duodenal) ulcer bleeding: gastroduodenal artery. (Book p155)

questions.q: Johnson's type I gastric ulcer is managed by:
opts: Distal gastrectomy with reconstruction (Billroth I or II)
questions.exp: Type I: distal gastrectomy + reconstruction (Billroth I or II). (Book p155)

questions.q: Surgical options for a type IV (high) gastric ulcer include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Type IV operations: Pauchet procedure, Kelling-Madlener procedure, Csendes procedure. (Book p156)

questions.q: The Csendes procedure for a high gastric ulcer is a:
questions.exp: Csendes procedure: Roux-en-Y esophagogastrojejunostomy. (Book p156)

questions.q: H. pylori is the common cause of:
questions.exp: H. pylori: common cause of gastric ulcer disease. (Book p156)

questions.q: The genes of H. pylori that encode for toxins are:
questions.exp: CagA, VacA: genes that encode for toxins. (Book p156)

questions.q: The enzyme that allows H. pylori to survive the acidic environment is:
questions.exp: Urease enzyme (+): survives acidic environment. (Book p156)

questions.q: H. pylori pathogenicity includes all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Pathogenicity: peptic ulcer, type B gastritis, gastric cancer, MALTomas. (Book p156)

questions.q: MALTomas associated with H. pylori are:
questions.exp: MALTomas: mucosal associated lymphoid tissue tumors. (Book p156)

questions.q: H. pylori infection is thought to be:
opts: Slightly protective against esophageal adenocarcinoma and GERD
A strong risk factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma
questions.exp: H. pylori is slightly protective against adenocarcinoma of the esophagus and GERD. (Book p156)

units.title: Stomach: Relevant Anatomy
units.guide: Four arteries feed the stomach - left gastric (direct off the coeliac axis, the dominant vessel, and the one that bleeds in a type IV gastric ulcer or a Mallory-Weiss tear), right gastric (common hepatic), right gastroepiploic (gastroduodenal) and the short gastrics (splenic). Because they anastomose freely in the submucosa, the stomach survives ligation of most of them.

units.title: Venous Drainage of the Stomach
units.sec: Venous Drainage of the Stomach · p151
units.guide: Gastric veins mirror the arteries, and the left gastric or coronary vein is the route by which gastric cancer seeds the liver.

units.title: Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis: Features
units.sec: Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis: Features · p151
units.guide: CHPS - idiopathic hypertrophic pyloric stenosis - is pyloric muscle hypertrophy causing gastric outlet obstruction, classically in a first-born boy between two and three weeks old, linked to Apert and Cornelia de Lange syndromes, low nitric oxide synthase and early erythromycin exposure. Feed the baby and watch: an olive mass is felt and peristaltic waves roll left to right.

units.title: CHPS: Differentials & Investigations
units.guide: Bilious vomiting from birth with a double bubble means duodenal atresia; non-bilious projectile vomiting after a few weeks means CHPS. Ultrasound is the IOC (muscle thickness >= 4 mm, elongated channel); contrast shows the string, mushroom and double-tract signs and the X-ray a single bubble.

units.title: CHPS: Metabolic Abnormalities
units.guide: Vomiting hydrochloric acid leaves behind hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic, hyponatraemic metabolic alkalosis. The kidney first spills bicarbonate, then the renin-angiotensin system drives aldosterone, sodium is reabsorbed at the cost of potassium and hydrogen - so the urine turns acid despite the alkalosis: paradoxical aciduria.

units.title: CHPS: Management
units.guide: Correct with Ringer lactate before Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy (split the muscle until the mucosa bulges). Feed at 4-6 hours if the operation was clean, at 24-48 hours if the mucosa was breached.

units.title: Peptic Ulcers: Types
units.guide: Duodenal ulcers are the commonest peptic ulcers: 90-95% H. pylori, acid hypersecretion, first part of the duodenum, pain that food relieves. Gastric ulcers are 60-65% H. pylori with normal acid output in types I and II.

units.title: Peptic Ulcer: Bleeding
units.guide: Bleeding is the commonest complication and comes from posterior duodenal ulcers eroding the gastroduodenal artery - the commonest cause of upper GI haemorrhage. Endoscopic adrenaline and coagulation first, repeat endoscopy once for a re-bleed, then surgery to under-run the vessel; eradicate H. pylori once it is quiet.

units.title: Peptic Ulcer: Perforation
units.guide: Perforation favours anterior ulcers and presents as peritonitis with gas under the diaphragm: resuscitate, antibiotics covering aerobes and anaerobes, analgesia and emergency Graham's omental patch. A posterior ulcer leaks backwards into the retroperitoneum - gas under the right kidney, Valentino syndrome mimicking appendicitis, and Kocherisation to see it.

units.title: Gastric Ulcers: Johnson's Classification
units.guide: Johnson's classification: type I along the lesser curvature near the incisura (commonest), type II prepyloric plus duodenal, type III prepyloric, type IV high in the body eroding the left gastric artery, type V NSAID-related and diffuse; types IV and V bleed.

units.title: Gastric Ulcer: Diagnosis & Management
units.guide: Gastric ulcer pain worsens with food and perforates more often than it bleeds. Endoscopy (with the U/J manoeuvre for fundal ulcers) must biopsy every gastric ulcer to exclude cancer. Type I needs a distal gastrectomy with Billroth I or II; high type IV ulcers need Pauchet, Kelling-Madlener or a Csendes Roux-en-Y esophagogastrojejunostomy.

units.title: Helicobacter pylori
units.guide: H. pylori drives gastric ulcer disease through CagA and VacA toxins and urease, which lets it live in acid; it causes peptic ulceration, type B gastritis, gastric cancer and MALTomas - yet is slightly protective against esophageal adenocarcinoma and reflux.
